title: Investor’s savings lost after ASIC call
full_text:
A Queensland woman who invested all her retirement savings into a little-known property fund, checked with the corporate watchdog before handing over her money and was told everything looked fine.
Three years later, the Global Capital Property Fund (GCPF) and its licensee, United Global Capital, had collapsed into liquidation.
All up, the fund raised about $93m from more than 500 investors between 2019 and 2024. By the end, most of the money was gone, blown on failed property projects, referral fees and management costs paid to a related entity.
What the woman couldn’t have known when she made that phone call in early 2021 was that UGC was already on the corporate watchdog’s radar, courtesy of Shield Master Fund’s Paul Chiodo.
When she was cold called about a “superannuation health check” in February 2021, Janelle Fisher* figured it would do no harm to hear out the person on the other end of the phone.
The sell was convincing. She was soon passed on to a United Global Capital adviser who was quick to talk up the benefits of a self-managed super fund, pointing to cost savings and higher returns.
The Melbourne-based GCPF was targeting 13 per cent returns compared to 2 per cent for the average fund, Ms Fisher was told.
In reality, super funds were having their best year on record, with the median fund returning 18 per cent that year following the 2020 Covid market meltdown.
Still, 60-year-old Ms Fisher was cautious. She called her accountant, consulted with a friend who knew about finance, and sent off a series of questions to the financial adviser, including about the investments and whether it was risky to put all of their money in property developments. Each time she was reassured.
“There will always be risk, however, your money along with other investors is diversified across all new projects nationally to mitigate the risk but also to give you an opportunity to maximise the potential returns so you don’t have all your eggs in one basket,” the adviser wrote back.
Before taking the plunge and handing over the $310,000 she and her husband had saved over their working lives, Ms Fisher did one final check.
She called the one place she felt she would get a clear, unbiased answer: the Australian Securities & Investments Commission.
“They’re going to take all of our super, it’s quite nerve-wracking,” Ms Fisher said on the call. The Australian has obtained a copy of the recording.
The ASIC representative confirmed the GCPF was registered and licensed by United Global Capital. All looked as it should. No suspensions, no red flags.
“Do I need to do any other research or is what I’m doing with you the best,” Ms Fisher asked.
“I don’t know if there’s a specialised super search you could do. As long as they’re registered and they’re licensed to deal in superannuation, that’s pretty much all you can check, as far as I’m aware,” the ASIC representative replied.
“If there are any issues and something goes wrong, then you know they’re regulated by us so you can lodge a formal complaint through ASIC or the Australian Financial Complaints Authority,” the representative said.
Encouraged by ASIC’s reassurances, Ms Fisher and her husband went ahead, putting all of their super into the GCPF.
When they tried to move their money out of the fund in late 2023, they were told they would have to wait for a buyer to purchase their holding. Five months later, they were able to get $50,000 out.
A second redemption request in the middle of 2024 was never honoured, and the fund collapsed soon after.
After going through the financial complaints ombudsman and Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, Ms Fisher and her husband have been compensated to the tune of $150,000, half of what they put into the fund.
“We weren’t reckless with our retirement savings,” Ms Fisher said. “I questioned the investment, I spoke to my accountant, and most importantly I contacted ASIC.
“I wanted to make sure we were dealing with people and an investment that was properly regulated. I was assured. What more is an ordinary Australian supposed to do?” Red flags Incredibly, while Ms Fisher was doing her due diligence on the GCPF in February 2021, ASIC’s misconduct and breach reporting team were exchanging emails with Shield’s Mr Chiodo, where he named UGC and the First Guardian Master Fund.
An email from Mr Chiodo to ASIC in January 2021 urged the regulator to investigate financial adviser Sharree Hutchinson for cold calling his investors and urging them to switch to the First Guardian fund.
This was after the fallout between First Guardian and Mr Chiodo that led him to start the Shield Master Fund.
She must have gotten his investor list from either First Guardian or United Global Capital, Mr Chiodo told the regulator in emails obtained by The Australian.
He then tells ASIC that his fund is for retail clients and he gives a glimpse of the scheme he was operating with UGC.
“UGC provides the SoA (statement of advice) for the clients entering our fund and set up the clients with SMSF should they not have one,” Mr Chiodo wrote.
“Most (of) our clients (approx 95 per cent) will not originally have a SMSF and UGC sets them up with a SMSF and then a SoA for investment on a portion of their superannuation amount into our fund. However, as the client have a SMSF, they no longer require a SoA to transfer their funds,” Mr Chiodo volunteered on the arrangement.
ASIC, it seems, failed to pick up on the potential red flag that retail investors were being funnelled into the Chiodo fund via UGC and ignored Mr Chiodo’s warnings about First Guardian.
A full year later, Mr Chiodo emailed ASIC again and warned of the same conduct. Again, he named First Guardian and UGC, as well as Ms Hutchinson’s advice shop, Funds United. He was told the investigation was ongoing.
A few months later he emailed again, warning of illegal activity at First Guardian. Again, the regulator failed to act.
Ms Hutchinson was eventually slapped with a six-year ban in late 2022, while ASIC put temporary stop orders on the GCPF and other United Global Capital funds through 2022 but only froze the assets of the fund in mid 2024. By this stage, most of the money was gone.
But no alarm bells rang at the regulator relating to Mr Chiodo or First Guardian.
ASIC was concerned about adviser conduct and cold calling but didn’t think to look beyond that to uncover where advisers were investing client money.
ASIC only began investigating the Shield fund in 2023, when it received reports of misconduct. That investigation led the regulator to First Guardian, which it began investigating in 2024.
It took until February 2025 for ASIC to freeze the First Guardian fund. The action came nine months after the fund had locked investors out of $500m in super savings by suspending redemptions.
First Guardian invested much of the money in companies associated with a director, David Anderson, while tens of millions were sent overseas, squandered on high-risk property deals that went nowhere.
Liquidators have so far only recovered about $6m, all of it gone on fees to both the liquidators and lawyers.
ASIC said inbound callers hear a recorded message urging them to seek professional advice and that its representatives are instructed not to provide advice of a legal or financial nature.
“ASIC receives thousands of reports of misconduct,” a spokeswoman said. “Reports of misconduct are assessed through ASIC’s regulatory and enforcement processes. Reports of misconduct are recorded on ASIC’s internal systems once they are triaged.
“ASIC is not in a position to inform members of the public when it has received reports of misconduct without first being in a position to verify whether those concerns are valid or legitimate. The existence of a report does not establish misconduct.” *A pseudonym has been used at the investor’s request but The Australian has sighted documents confirming her investment in the GCPF in 2021 as well as contact with the UGC financial adviser.
